subject: maths
title: Chapter 3 · Test 2
summary: Fifteen questions on Pythagoras’ theorem in 2D and 3D, the trigonometric ratios, finding sides and angles, and angles of elevation and depression.
body: This test covers Chapter 3: Pythagoras’ theorem (in 2D and 3D), the trigonometric ratios, finding side lengths and angles with trigonometry, and angles of elevation and depression. It has 15 questions, from easy to challenge. Allow about 25 minutes and work with no notes. You need a scientific calculator for this chapter — set it to degree mode before you start. Diagrams are drawn to scale, but always calculate rather than measure. Sketch and label the right-angled triangle for each question, round only at the end, and give the units.

questions.prompt: A gate is 2.0 m wide and 1.5 m high. How long is the diagonal brace d across it?
questions.explanation: d² = 1.5² + 2² = 6.25, so d = 2.5 m. Adding the lengths (3.5) skips the squaring.
steps: d is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse: d² = 1.5² + 2².

mistakes.A: Step 2: you added the lengths. Square each side first, then add.
mistakes.B: Step 3: 6.25 is d². Take the square root.
mistakes.D: Step 2: to find the hypotenuse, add the squares — don’t subtract them.

questions.diagram_alt: A rectangular gate 2.0 m wide and 1.5 m high with a diagonal brace d.

questions.prompt: In triangle XYZ, the right angle is at Y and θ is at Z. Which side is adjacent to θ?
questions.explanation: YZ touches θ at Z and isn’t the hypotenuse, so it is the adjacent side. XZ also touches Z, but it is the hypotenuse.
steps: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle at Y: XZ.
The sides touching θ at Z are XZ and YZ.
XZ is the hypotenuse, so the adjacent side is YZ.

mistakes.B: Step 3: XY doesn’t touch θ at Z — it is the opposite side.
mistakes.C: Step 1: XZ is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse, even though it touches Z.
mistakes.D: Step 3: only one side is adjacent: the side that touches Z and is not the hypotenuse.

questions.diagram_alt: Triangle XYZ with the right angle at Y and the angle θ marked at Z.

questions.prompt: Find x, the side opposite the 48° angle, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: tan 48° = x/10, so x = 10 × tan 48° ≈ 11.11 cm. 9.00 cm comes from doing the opposite operation (x is on top).
steps: Label from the 48° angle: 10 cm is the adjacent; x is the opposite.
Adjacent and opposite means TOA: tan 48° = x/10.

mistakes.A: Step 3: x is on top in the equation, so multiply — you did the opposite.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you used sin. With the adjacent and the opposite, the ratio is tan (TOA).
mistakes.C: Step 2: you used cos. With the adjacent and the opposite, the ratio is tan (TOA).

questions.diagram_alt: A right-angled triangle with a 48° angle, adjacent side 10 cm and opposite side x.

questions.prompt: Sam looks down from a bridge at a boat. What is the angle θ in the diagram called?

options.C: The angle between the line of sight and the bridge pillar

questions.explanation: θ is measured down from the horizontal at Sam’s eye to the line of sight, so it is the angle of depression.
steps: Find θ: it is at Sam, between the dashed horizontal line and the line of sight.
Sam is looking down at the boat.
Looking down from the horizontal is an angle of depression.

mistakes.A: Step 2: Sam is looking DOWN at the boat, so it is an angle of depression.
mistakes.C: Step 1: θ is measured from the dashed horizontal line, not from the vertical pillar.
mistakes.D: Step 1: the right angle is at the bottom of the pillar. θ is between the horizontal and the line of sight.

questions.diagram_alt: Sam on a bridge looking down at a boat, with a dashed horizontal line at Sam’s eye and the angle θ down to the line of sight.

questions.prompt: Find x as an exact answer (a surd).
questions.explanation: x² = 7² − 3² = 40, so x = √40 cm. Adding the squares would make x longer than the hypotenuse.
steps: 7 cm is the hypotenuse, so x² = 7² − 3².

mistakes.A: Step 1: 7 is the hypotenuse, so subtract: 7² − 3².
mistakes.B: Step 2: you subtracted the lengths. Square them first.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 40 is x². The exact answer keeps the square root sign.

questions.diagram_alt: A right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 7 cm, one shorter side 3 cm and the other shorter side x.

questions.prompt: A cylindrical tube has a diameter of 16 cm and a height of 30 cm. Find the length x of the longest straight rod that fits inside.
questions.explanation: x² = 16² + 30² = 256 + 900 = 1156, so x = 34 cm. Using the radius gives about 31.0 cm.
steps: The rod goes across the diameter and up the height, which meet at a right angle.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the rod crosses the whole width. Use the diameter (16 cm), not the radius (8 cm).
mistakes.C: Step 2: you added the lengths 16 + 30. Square them first.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 1156 is x². Take the square root.

questions.diagram_alt: A cylinder with diameter 16 cm and height 30 cm with the longest rod x drawn inside.

questions.prompt: Write sin θ for the triangle shown.
questions.explanation: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse = 40/41. 9/41 uses the wrong pair of sides.
steps: Label from θ: opposite = 40, adjacent = 9, hypotenuse = 41.
SOH: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.

mistakes.B: Step 2: 9/41 is cos θ (CAH). Sin is SOH.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 40/9 is tan θ (TOA). Sin is SOH.
mistakes.D: Step 3: the fraction is upside down. In SOH, the opposite goes on top.

questions.diagram_alt: A right-angled triangle with 9 m next to θ, 40 m across from θ and hypotenuse 41 m.

questions.prompt: Find θ, the angle opposite the 5 cm side, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: sin θ = 5/9, so θ = sin⁻¹(5/9) ≈ 33.7°. 56.3° is the other acute angle, which you get from the wrong ratio or the fraction upside down.
steps: Label from θ: 5 is the opposite and 9 is the hypotenuse.
SOH: sin θ = 5/9.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the 5 side is the opposite, so use sin, not cos. Your answer is the other acute angle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 9 is the hypotenuse. Tan doesn’t use the hypotenuse — use sin.
mistakes.D: Step 2: tan needs two shorter sides, but 9 is the hypotenuse. Use sin θ = 5/9.

questions.diagram_alt: A right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 9 cm and the side opposite θ equal to 5 cm.

questions.prompt: The side opposite the 41° angle is 8.5 m. Find the hypotenuse x, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation: sin 41° = 8.5/x, so x = 8.5 ÷ sin 41° ≈ 12.96 m. 5.58 m comes from doing the opposite operation (x is on the bottom).
steps: Label from the 41° angle: 8.5 m is the opposite; x is the hypotenuse.
Opposite and hypotenuse means SOH: sin 41° = 8.5/x.

mistakes.A: Step 3: x is on the bottom in the equation, so divide — you did the opposite.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you used cos. With the opposite and the hypotenuse, the ratio is sin (SOH).
mistakes.C: Step 2: you used tan. With the opposite and the hypotenuse, the ratio is sin (SOH).

questions.diagram_alt: A right-angled triangle with a 41° angle, the opposite side 8.5 m and the hypotenuse x.

questions.prompt: A tree casts an 18 m shadow when the angle of elevation of the sun is 40°. How tall is the tree, to 1 decimal place?
questions.explanation: tan 40° = x/18, so x = 18 × tan 40° ≈ 15.1 m. 21.5 m comes from doing the opposite operation (x is on top).
steps: Label from the 40° angle: 18 m is the adjacent; x is the opposite.
Adjacent and opposite means TOA: tan 40° = x/18.

mistakes.B: Step 3: x is on top in the equation, so multiply — you did the opposite.
mistakes.C: Step 2: you used sin. With the adjacent and the opposite, the ratio is tan (TOA).
mistakes.D: Step 2: you used cos. With the adjacent and the opposite, the ratio is tan (TOA).

questions.diagram_alt: A tree with an 18 m shadow; the sun’s angle of elevation from the tip of the shadow to the top of the tree is 40°; the tree’s height is x.

questions.prompt: A ramp 4 m long rises 0.9 m. Find the angle θ the ramp makes with the ground, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: sin θ = 0.9/4, so θ = sin⁻¹(0.9/4) ≈ 13.0°. 77.0° is the other acute angle, which you get from the wrong ratio or the fraction upside down.
steps: Label from θ: 0.9 is the opposite and 4 is the hypotenuse.
SOH: sin θ = 0.9/4.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the 0.9 side is the opposite, so use sin, not cos. Your answer is the other acute angle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 4 is the hypotenuse. Tan doesn’t use the hypotenuse — use sin.
mistakes.D: Step 2: tan needs two shorter sides, but 4 is the hypotenuse. Use sin θ = 0.9/4.

questions.diagram_alt: A ramp drawn as a right-angled triangle: the sloping ramp is 4 m, the rise is 0.9 m, and θ is the angle with the ground.

questions.prompt: A square pyramid has a base side of 8 cm and a slant height s = 9 cm (from the middle of a base edge to the top). Find its vertical height h, to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: From the centre to the middle of an edge is 4 cm, so h² = 9² − 4² = 81 − 16 = 65 and h = √65 ≈ 8.1 cm.
steps: The centre of the base is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm from the middle of each edge.
The slant height (9 cm) is the hypotenuse: h² = 9² − 4² = 81 − 16 = 65.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the height meets the centre, which is half the side (4 cm) from the middle of an edge — not 8 cm.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the slant height is the hypotenuse, so subtract: 9² − 4².
mistakes.D: Step 1: you used half the base diagonal (√32), which goes to a corner. The slant height goes to the middle of an edge: use 4 cm.

questions.diagram_alt: A square pyramid with base side 8 cm, slant height s (9 cm) from the middle of a base edge to the top, and vertical height h.

questions.prompt: An equilateral triangle has sides of 10 cm. Find its height h, to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: The height cuts the base into 5 cm halves, so h² = 10² − 5² = 75 and h = √75 ≈ 8.7 cm.
steps: The height meets the base at a right angle and cuts it in half: 5 cm.
In the right-angled half, 10 cm is the hypotenuse: h² = 10² − 5² = 100 − 25 = 75.

mistakes.A: Step 2: the 10 cm side is the hypotenuse, so subtract 5² — don’t add.
mistakes.B: Step 2: you subtracted the lengths 10 − 5. Square them first.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 75 is h². Take the square root.

questions.diagram_alt: An equilateral triangle with sides 10 cm and a dashed height h from the top to the middle of the base.

questions.prompt: A walking track climbs in two straight sections: first 250 m at 12° to the horizontal, then 180 m at 20° to the horizontal. How much height is gained in total, to 1 decimal place?
steps: Section 1: the 250 m track is the hypotenuse; the rise is opposite 12°: 250 × sin 12° ≈ 51.98 m.
Section 2: 180 × sin 20° ≈ 61.56 m.

mistakes.A: Step 1: each section is a hypotenuse, so the rise is length × sin, not length × tan.
mistakes.C: Step 1: you can’t average the angles. Work out each section’s rise separately and add them.
mistakes.D: Step 1: cos gives the horizontal distance. The rise is opposite the angle, so use sin.

questions.diagram_alt: A track made of two straight sections: 250 m at 12° to the horizontal, then 180 m at 20° to the horizontal.

questions.prompt: A hot-air balloon is directly above point P. From Q, 600 m from P on level ground, the angle of elevation of the balloon is 28°. The balloon then rises straight up another 100 m. Find the new angle of elevation from Q, to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation: First height = 600 × tan 28° ≈ 319.03 m. New height ≈ 419.03 m. New angle = tan⁻¹(419.03 ÷ 600) ≈ 34.9°.
steps: First height: tan 28° = h/600, so h = 600 × tan 28° ≈ 319.03 m.

mistakes.B: Step 3: you can’t add angles. Find the new height, then use tan⁻¹(new height ÷ 600).
mistakes.C: Step 3: 600 m is the horizontal distance (adjacent), not the line of sight. Use tan⁻¹, not sin⁻¹.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the new height is the old height plus 100 m, not just 100 m.

questions.diagram_alt: A balloon above P, 600 m from Q. The first line of sight from Q is at 28°; the balloon then rises 100 m to a new position, with the new line of sight from Q dashed.
